analysis.one_liner: Caps what patients pay out of pocket for insulin at $25 a month and bans insurers from requiring prior authorization for it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced in January 2023, it sat in the Senate HELP committee for the rest of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required health insurance plans — employer plans, individual plans, and Medicare's drug benefit — to cover insulin with a monthly out-of-pocket cap of $25 per 30-day supply. It would also have banned insurers from requiring prior authorization or step therapy (trying cheaper drugs first) for covered insulins, and would have lowered the Medicare insulin cap from $35 to $25 a month. It was referred to the Senate HELP committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million Americans who use insulin and get it through employer plans, individual plans, or Medicare: their monthly out-of-pocket insulin cost would be capped at $25, the deductible would not apply, and insurers could not make them jump through prior-authorization or step-therapy hoops for covered insulins. High-deductible plan enrollees benefit most, since insulin coverage would count before the deductible is met.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users with private or Medicare insurance

how_it_helps.text: Caps private-insurance cost-sharing for a month's supply of covered insulin at $25, or 25% of the negotiated price after rebates if lower, and eliminates the deductible for those products, starting in 2024.
Lowers the Medicare Part D insulin copay cap from $35 per month to $25, and prohibits insurers from requiring prior authorization or step therapy for covered insulins unless clinically justified.
Requires catastrophic health plans to cover selected insulin before the deductible is met, which matters for high-deductible plan enrollees who otherwise pay full price.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans, which would absorb the difference between patients' $25 copay and the negotiated insulin price, plus pharmacy benefit managers and drugmakers who would face a smaller payer clampdown; some of that cost would likely flow back into premiums for all enrollees.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay, not what manufacturers charge; it lowers cost-sharing out of plan funds, which could add modestly to insurance premiums, and it does nothing to bring down insulin list prices themselves.

Coverage mandates apply only to the 'selected' products each plan chooses to count, plans may still charge more for insulin obtained from out-of-network providers, and the cost-sharing exemption for catastrophic plans is excluded from actuarial-value calculations — carve-outs that narrow the benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: diabetics on employer or individual plans would see their insulin cost-sharing capped at $25 and lose prior-authorization and step-therapy hurdles for selected insulins, and Medicare beneficiaries' cap would drop from $35 to $25 [S2]. The costs are modest but real: those amounts come out of insurance risk pools rather than from manufacturers, so premiums could rise slightly, and the bill addresses out-of-pocket cost-sharing while leaving list prices untouched — a narrower approach than capping manufacturer prices directly. It is a simple, well-designed patient-cost fix, but it is also a small-claims version of a larger problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee and died there without ever being scheduled for a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the Cap Insulin Prices Act on January 30, 2023, with one Democratic cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate HELP committee.
The Senate Banking committee held a hearing that touched on the bill in June 2024, but the HELP committee, which controlled the bill, never acted on it.
No committee vote, floor vote, or House action ever occurred; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers are better off: the requirement to cover insulin at no more than $25 per month with no prior-authorization hurdles never took effect, and drugmakers keep the existing cost-sharing structure.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the Senate in January 2023.

for.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing in June 2024 at which the subject was examined (S.Hrg. 118-558), the only committee activity beyond referral.

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral for the entire 118th Congress without a markup or vote, allowing it to die there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a Democratic cosponsor, but the bill never advanced far enough for any vote to reveal a partisan split.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans must absorb the cost of insulin above the $25 cap for covered products and drop prior-authorization and step-therapy requirements, which could nudge premiums up for everyone. The bill shifts a slice of drug cost from diabetic patients to insurance risk pools.

The cost-sharing cap is computed on the negotiated price net of all rebates, including PBM-side concessions, limiting how much of the middleman discount can be excluded when counting what patients pay — a direct hit to a PBM revenue practice — while leaving the rebate system itself untouched.

The bill does not cap what manufacturers charge for insulin — only what patients pay out of pocket — so drugmakers keep their list prices and rebate arrangements while the cost of expensive insulin continues to flow through insurers and premiums.
